book: 143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul

chapters.file: ch03 - The Blackwell Philosophy and Pop Culture Series.md
ch09 - PART ONE - DOES THE DARK KNIGHT ALWAYS DO RIGHT.md

chapters.relation: Mark D. White asks why Batman refuses to kill the Joker even after the Joker murdered Jason Todd, paralyzed Barbara Gordon, and killed Sarah Essen. Framing the refusal as deontological rather than utilitarian, he runs the case through Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and transplant case, arguing the classics disanalogize because the Joker himself creates the danger and because 'do not kill' is an agent-specific rule rather than an agent-neutral one. He extends the analysis to prepunishment via Philip K. Dick's Minority Report, and concedes that even a self-described strict deontologist can conclude Batman maybe should have killed the Joker years ago.

James DiGiovanna asks whether it was right for Batman to turn street kids Dick Grayson and Jason Todd into Robin. He tests the training against Kant's universalizability (including the Joker-demanding-to-know-where-Robin-is lie example), against Bentham and Mill's utilitarian appeal to Gotham's general good, and finally reads it through the virtue ethics of Plato, Aristotle, and MacIntyre's After Virtue, where Robin is trained into a role-specific character rather than taught rules. Jason's rashness and death at the Joker's hands show Batman failed to moderate his ward's courage, and the chapter concludes Batman is 'a lousy deontologist, a decent consequentialist, and some kind of virtue ethicist.'

Stephen Kershnar argues that Batman's hatred of criminals is not a vice but a virtue, since hating what is evil is the morally appropriate attitude toward wrongdoers like the Joker or Batman: Year One's brutal Detective Flass. Against Aristotle's person-focused Virtuous-Persons Theory he defends a 'Virtuous-Thoughts-and-Actions Theory,' illustrated by Gordon's retaliatory beating of Flass and Batman elbow-smashing a pimp in Year One. The chapter closes on the golden mean of balanced love and hate: Batman's virtuous hatred leaves his life isolated and unflourishing, showing that virtue does not guarantee eudaimonia.

chapters.file: ch13 - PART TWO - LAW, JUSTICE, AND THE SOCIAL ORDER WHERE DOES BATMAN FIT IN.md

chapters.relation: Brett Chandler Patterson reads the No Man's Land storyline, in which earthquake-isolated Gotham is carved into gang territories by Two-Face, Penguin, and the Joker, alongside Hurricane Katrina's flooding of New Orleans as twin real-and-fictional tests of Hobbes's state of nature and the social contract. He contrasts Jim Gordon's lawful, Machiavellian-seeming rebuilding of trust with Officer William Petit's slide into execution-style 'despotic' power, and highlights the pacifist witness of Father Christian and Dr. Leslie Thompkins against Hobbes's demand that churches defer to the sovereign. Batman's turn as a benevolent gang lord working to hand the city back to Gordon shows, for Patterson, that Batman's real enemy is anarchy itself.

Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive. Working from Max Weber's definition of the state as monopoly on legitimate violence, Hobbes's Leviathan, and Nietzsche's state as 'new idol,' he reads Year One's corrupt Commissioner Loeb, Year Two's self-appointed Reaper, Anarky's failed anarchist dystopia, Two-Face's broken faith in the law, and The Dark Knight Returns' state-loyal Superman and Commissioner Yindel. The Batman-Gordon partnership emerges as a precarious unofficial order in which Gordon tolerates the one exception to the state's monopoly on violence.

chapters.file: ch16 - Who Has the Last Laugh.md
chapters.relation: Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.

chapters.file: ch17 - PART THREE - ORIGINS AND ETHICS BECOMING THE CAPED CRUSADER.md

chapters.relation: Randall Jensen examines the boyhood promise Bruce made after his parents' murder ('I swear by the spirits of my parents... to avenge their deaths by spending the rest of my life warring on all criminals') and argues it is a backward-looking, deontological moral reason that consequentialism cannot accommodate. He then asks whether a promise to the dead can bind at all, weighing Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us against Aristotle's and Thomas Nagel's postmortem and unexperienced harms, concluding Bruce wrongs the living people Thomas and Martha Wayne were if he breaks it. From The Dark Knight Returns to Kingdom Come, Batman emerges as a man who can never fully keep the promise yet cannot live without it.

Mahesh Ananth and Ben Dixon pit young Bruce Wayne against Peter Singer: given seven billion dollars, Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' principle, illustrated by the drowning child, seems to require giving nearly everything to famine relief rather than dressing up as a bat. Against appeals to honoring his parents' memory and to supererogation, the authors deploy Singer's strong and moderate versions of giving and utilitarian indifference to distance, concluding that a true utilitarian would forbid becoming Batman. The irony they highlight is that the older Batman himself reasons utilitarianly when he abandons Jason Todd to intercept the Joker's poisoned convoy in A Death in the Family.

chapters.file: ch20 - Batman Is a Moral Exemplar.md
chapters.relation: Ryan Indy Rhodes and David Kyle Johnson defend Batman as a genuine moral exemplar whose justice, beneficence, generosity, and courage (from reprinting No Man's Land land deeds to sacrificing his reputation in Batman Begins) are worth emulating even though no one can copy his feats. They rebut the unrealistic objection, the language objection that 'Batman is virtuous' lacks a truthmaker (likening it to 'dragons breathe fire'), and the exaggeration objection by noting that exemplars like Buddha, Jesus, and Socrates reach us through embellished, partly fictional depictions anyway. Fiction even helps, since we can read Batman's thought balloons, and his growth into an 'icon' supplies the stable true character that emulation requires.

chapters.file: ch21 - PART FOUR - WHO IS THE BATMAN (IS THAT A TRICK QUESTION ).md
ch22 - Can You Face the Bat.md
chapters.relation: Sarah Donovan and Nicholas Richardson use Nietzsche and Foucault to present Batman as a self-constructed identity: across Batman: Year One, Arkham Asylum, and The Dark Knight Returns, Bruce consciously builds the persona ('Yes, Father, I shall become a bat') rather than revealing a deeper true self. Foucault's constructed categories of normal and abnormal surface in Arkham Asylum's 'super-sane' Joker and the Alice in Wonderland parallels that put Batman's own sanity in question alongside Amadeus Arkham's madness. Nietzsche's will to power and eternal recurrence, via the shepherd biting the snake in Zarathustra, explain why Bruce can face the bat that others flee, becoming heroic where Arkham and Dr. Cavendish go insane.

chapters.file: ch23 - All Joking Aside, This Is a Modal Muddle.md
chapters.relation: Sam Cowling and Chris Ragg ask whether Batman could have been the Joker, using the Indiscernibility of Identicals and the Necessity of Identity over possible worlds to argue that if 'Batman' is a name of a merely possible individual, he could not have been identical to the Joker. The 'Robin argument' (many people have been Robin) pushes back that 'Batman' might be a disguised description, and the authors then treat Batman and the Joker as abstract fictional characters whose modal properties are stipulated by their authors. On that view the Elseworlds tale Batman: Two-Faces, where the two are literally one Jekyll-and-Hyde person, shows Batman could have been the Joker after all.

chapters.file: ch24 - Keeping It in the Family.md
chapters.relation: Jason Southworth deploys counterexamples, from Golden Age Batman shooting the vampire Monk with silver bullets, through Jean-Paul Valley and Dick Grayson serving as Batman during Knightfall and Prodigal, to the Frankenstein twist of Castle of the Bat and the criminal Batman of Earth-A, to show that nothing (not being Bruce Wayne, not never killing, not murdered parents) is necessary or sufficient for being Batman. Turning to Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations, he applies family resemblance and the game examples: 'Batman' works like 'game,' identified through overlapping similarities rather than a fixed definition. Retconned Robins and disappearing Batarangs show language works without fixed meanings, which he warns undermines using Batman as a determinate moral exemplar.

chapters.file: ch25 - What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum.md
chapters.relation: Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.

chapters.file: ch26 - PART FIVE - BEING THE BAT INSIGHTS FROM EXISTENTIALISM AND TAOISM.md

chapters.relation: Christopher Drohan reads Batman and Alfred through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Batman, like Abraham, believes 'by virtue of the absurd,' resigning himself to an infinite, never-realizable justice as a knight of infinite resignation, while Alfred embodies the higher knight of faith whose justice is concrete love expressed in mending the suit, making sandwiches, and guarding the manor. Heidegger's thrownness and Sartre's condemned freedom frame both men's absurd existential condition, including Batman sparing Joe Chill and even allying with him against the Reaper. The chapter's verdict is that Alfred's faithful devotion to one person is the superior ethic, and that peace begins with him.

Jason Howard asks how Batman keeps from becoming what he fights, answering with Heidegger's authentic conscience against Rousseau's innate moral-sense view. Bruce's guilt over his parents' death is reinterpreted in a Heideggerian 'moment of vision': the bat through the window summons Dasein out of the they-self, so becoming Batman is not vengeance but the call of an authentic conscience that owns guilt, fallenness, and death. Batman's return from alcoholic retirement in The Dark Knight Returns shows conscience as 'the loyalty of existence to its own Self,' a freedom-toward-death that makes him instructive rather than merely heroic.

chapters.file: ch29 - Determinism and the Dark Knight.md
chapters.relation: David Hart uses Heidegger to dissolve the question of whether Batman is determined by childhood trauma or freely chooses his mission. Heidegger's being-in-the-world and thrown-project, illustrated by Alfred the butler for whom the clock is essentially something to dust, replace the subject-object picture that grounds both free-will and determinism talk. Read this way, the bat crashing through the window in Batman: Year One is Bruce's Angst-laden confrontation with death as 'the possibility of my own impossibility,' through which he freely takes up the project of being Batman when nothing forced him to.

chapters.file: ch30 - PART SIX - FRIEND, FATHER, . . . RIVAL THE MANY ROLES OF THE BAT.md

chapters.relation: Galen Foresman arms Bat-fans with value theory: most evaluative comparisons of Batman and Superman beg the question, since Super-fans load pros-and-cons lists with superpowers and Bat-fans with intelligence without independently justifying why those traits count. He then argues that bravery is essential to superhero greatness, because the brave person knowingly confronts danger, so the powerless, bulletable Batman is systematically braver than the nearly invulnerable Superman. The conclusion inverts the fans' debate: the very superpowers Super-fans celebrate are what disqualify Superman from being the better hero.

Daniel Malloy argues Batman and Superman are friends who disagree about friendship itself: Superman practices Aristotle's highest philia between good men who are 'another self' and true equals, symbolized by the kryptonite ring he trusts Batman to use on him should he go rogue, while Batman's friendship is Nietzschean, loving in his friend the overman 'as your cause' in the one equal he respects as a rival. Stories like Tower of Babel, Bruce Wayne: Fugitive, and the Brother Eye satellite show Batman manipulates everyone except this one peer, and that he never fights Superman fairly because he does not need to. Their fundamental, unresolvable differences, Malloy concludes, are exactly what strengthen the World's Finest friendship.

chapters.file: ch33 - Leaving the Shadow of the Bat.md
chapters.relation: Carsten Fogh Nielsen stages Aristotle against Kant on moral education: Aristotle says we become just by doing just acts and imitating exemplary people, as Robin imitates Batman, while Kant objects that every example must first be appraised by principles of morality and that imitation breeds heteronomy rather than autonomy. The Gordon-Yindel disagreement over Batman in The Dark Knight Returns shows people can genuinely clash about who counts as morally exemplary in the first place. Dick Grayson resolves the tension by using the courage, skills, and integrity Batman instilled in him to stand up to Batman and become Nightwing, proving emulation can be the route to, not the enemy of, Kantian autonomy.

The book's final chapter is a mock interview in which 'Bat-Tzu' applies Taoism to Bruce Wayne's life: his yang (hard, retributive crime-fighting) has dominated his yin (his tenderness toward Dick, Tim, and Helena), and Robin has always been the yin balancing the Dark Knight. Quoting Lao-Tzu's Tao Te Ching and Chuang-Tzu on duality, acceptance of death (Jason Todd's resurrection), and effortlessness, the piece casts Alfred as the Taoist sage whose help exemplifies wu-wei, like Chuang-Tzu's butcher who cuts without dulling his blade. It even reads Batman's most intimidating feature, his absent shadow, as proof that nothingness can matter more than substance.

holes.name: Max Weber
holes.what: German sociologist and social theorist who defined the modern state as the institution that successfully claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its entire Batman-versus-the-state analysis on Weber's monopoly-of-legitimate-violence definition, explicitly contrasting it with Hobbes's Leviathan and Nietzsche's new idol.

holes.name: Family Resemblance
holes.what: Wittgenstein's idea that the things a general term applies to share no single common essence but are connected by overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, like the members of a family.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central claim is that there are no necessary and sufficient conditions for being Batman and that 'Batman' is identified only through Wittgensteinian family resemblance, which the existing language-games slug does not name.

holes.name: Knight of Faith (vs knight of infinite resignation)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling distinction between the knight of infinite resignation, who renounces the finite for an eternal ideal, and the knight of faith, who by virtue of the absurd repossesses the ordinary through passionate devotion.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire argument is that Batman is a knight of infinite resignation while Alfred is the higher knight of faith, a distinction no existing Kierkegaard slug (leap of faith, despair, anxiety) captures.
